paragraphs: Predicting protein side chains is one part of the larger protein-folding problem. This paper connects that task to probabilistic inference: finding the side-chain arrangement with minimum energy is equivalent to inference in an undirected graphical model. The resulting graph has relatively few connections but contains many cycles, making it a useful setting for studying approximate inference.

The authors use this connection to compare belief propagation, generalized belief propagation, and naive mean field on a concrete scientific problem. They give particular attention to max-product belief propagation, which searches for a best configuration. Where exact inference is feasible, it provides a reference for checking whether an approximate method reaches the true minimum.

In those tractable cases, max-product belief propagation found the global minimum whenever it converged, with a few convergence failures. Across the full protein dataset, it found lower-energy configurations than the other tested algorithms, including SCWRL. These results support its effectiveness on the studied task while preserving the distinction between strong observed performance and guaranteed convergence.
neurips-2002-approximate-inference-and-p.tldr: Protein side-chain prediction becomes a graphical-model inference problem, where max-product belief propagation performs strongly in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Many probabilistic learning methods share a smaller collection of underlying algorithmic ideas. This paper uses that common structure to automate the derivation of learning algorithms. Its AUTO BAYES system starts with a high-level statistical model specification and produces both a specialized algorithm and executable code that implements it.

The system combines reusable algorithmic schemas with symbolic program synthesis and computer algebra. These tools let it work through the mathematical structure of a model and tailor the resulting computation to that structure. The intended benefit is that a new model need not always require someone to manually derive and program a new learning procedure.

The authors present automatically derived solutions ranging from closed-form Bayesian textbook examples to EM algorithms for clustering, regression, and a multinomial version of principal component analysis. These examples illustrate a scope beyond selecting a routine from a fixed library. The contribution is a model-to-code process that can generate specialized, commented implementations for different languages or systems.
neurips-2002-automatic-derivation-of-sta.tldr: AUTO BAYES turns statistical model specifications into specialized learning algorithms and executable code using symbolic derivation.

paragraphs: This paper presents a physical neural-network system that recognizes patterns of visual motion and can learn to classify them online. Its front end is an analog VLSI optical-flow chip that computes global two-dimensional motion in real time. The system therefore begins with a hardware representation of movement in the visual input.

A central simplification converts continuous motion trajectories into sequences of motion events. Classification then operates on those event sequences, reducing the complexity of handling a continuously changing path. Apart from the optical-flow chip, the network structures use a winner-take-all architecture. The authors describe the complete system through the dynamics of these physical networks.

The demonstrated application is a contactless interface in which a person writes letters through visible motion. This connects the sensing and classification components to a recognizable interaction task. Based on the system's simplicity, robustness, and existing front end, the authors argue that a complete analog chip implementation is realistic, with potential uses in mobile electronics.
neurips-2002-classifying-patterns-of-vis.tldr: A neuromorphic system learns visual-motion patterns online by converting continuous trajectories into simpler event sequences.

paragraphs: Classification problems can ask for different kinds of outputs: one winning class, several applicable labels, or a ranking. This paper brings these settings into a common constraint-classification framework. The central idea is to express their learning requirements in a form that a shared method can handle, despite the different outputs each task requests.

The authors present a meta-algorithm that learns within this framework using one linear classifier in a high-dimensional space. This gives the framework a concrete computational route rather than leaving it as a way to describe related problems. The high-dimensional representation supports a common learning mechanism across the included classification and ranking settings.

The paper also examines generalization through distribution-independent and margin-based bounds, linking the framework to theoretical questions about performance beyond the training examples. It reports both empirical and theoretical evidence of benefits over existing multiclass classification methods. Together, these contributions support constraint classification as a unified approach with demonstrated advantages, without establishing that it wins in every included task.
neurips-2002-constraint-classification-f.tldr: Constraint classification unifies multiclass prediction, multilabel prediction, and ranking through a single high-dimensional linear classifier.

paragraphs: When several self-interested participants learn together, the choice of learning algorithm can itself become a strategic decision. This paper introduces efficient learning equilibrium to address that issue. It requires the learning procedures themselves to be in equilibrium, making incentives during learning part of the solution concept rather than considering only the eventual outcome.

Efficiency adds two requirements: the algorithms reach a desired value within polynomial time, and departing from the prescribed learning behavior becomes irrational within polynomial time. The concept therefore combines a computational requirement with a strategic one. A learning process must both deliver its target value efficiently and become resistant to beneficial deviations.

The authors prove existence under perfect monitoring, with the target set to the expected payoff of a Nash equilibrium. Under imperfect monitoring, such an equilibrium need not exist, although it does exist for common-interest games. They also extend their results to general stochastic games. These distinctions show that monitoring conditions and the alignment of participants' interests matter to the existence claims.
neurips-2002-efficient-learning-equilibr.tldr: Efficient learning equilibrium combines strategic stability with polynomial-time learning, with existence depending on monitoring and game structure.

paragraphs: Complex data can contain several competing kinds of structure, only some of which matter for a particular task. The information bottleneck approach addresses relevance by preserving information about an auxiliary variable. This paper observes that the auxiliary variable may itself include unwanted structure, so preserving information about it can retain more than the task needs.

The proposed formulation also minimizes information about another variable designated as irrelevant. This makes explicit knowledge of what to discard useful during feature extraction. It is particularly appealing when unwanted variation is easier to identify than the desired structure. The authors provide both a formal solution and an algorithmic treatment of this combined objective.

They demonstrate the method on a synthetic example and on problems involving text categorization and face images. The theoretical connection is to rate-distortion theory with side information: selecting a representation involves both retaining relevant content and suppressing specified irrelevant content. The contribution is a way to use both kinds of guidance when deciding which patterns in complex data to extract.
neurips-2002-extracting-relevant-structu.tldr: Feature extraction can use explicit information about unwanted variation alongside information about what the task should preserve.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction represents high-dimensional samples through a smaller set of coordinates. For visual data, the task becomes more complicated when appearance also changes through translations or rotations. Mixtures of transformation-invariant component analyzers address these changes while also clustering samples and learning local appearance deformations through dimensionality reduction.

The obstacle addressed here is the computational burden of learning that model with EM. The paper introduces fast Fourier transforms as a way to reduce the required computation. This targets the practical cost of fitting a model that already combines several useful capabilities, making its treatment of transformations and appearance variation more usable.

With the resulting speedup, the authors demonstrate the model in tracking, video textures, clustering video sequences, object recognition, and object detection in images. These applications illustrate the range of visual tasks that can benefit from the accelerated computation. The stated contribution is both an algorithmic acceleration and evidence that the faster model is effective across these applications.
neurips-2002-fast-transformation-invaria.tldr: Fast Fourier transforms accelerate transformation-invariant factor analysis, enabling demonstrations across several visual learning tasks.

paragraphs: Scientific datasets often describe relationships between pairs of objects rather than giving each object a conventional feature vector. Noise or unreliable estimates can make those relationships violate metric properties, complicating their use with standard learning methods. This paper develops a two-stage route from such pairwise measurements to a denoised metric representation.

First, the authors propose a vector embedding as an alternative to multidimensional scaling. This representation makes classical machine-learning and signal-processing tools available. It also preserves cluster assignments for a particular class of pairwise grouping algorithms: those with the stated shift-invariance property. That qualification matters because the preservation result is tied to this algorithmic property.

Second, denoising methods operate on the new vector representation. The authors provide theoretical control over both stages, connecting the original pairwise data to the cleaned metric form. They demonstrate the approach by finding structure in protein sequence databases and report visibly improved performance over existing automatic methods. The work thus links a representation argument to a practical denoising application.
neurips-2002-going-metric-denoising-pair.tldr: A vector embedding followed by denoising converts problematic pairwise data into a metric representation with useful preservation properties.

paragraphs: Gene expression profiles contain many measurements, while biological knowledge supplies relationships between genes. This paper combines those sources to extract useful features. Its graph connects genes known to take part in successive reactions in metabolic pathways, giving the algorithm information about biological relationships beyond the expression measurements themselves.

The motivating intuition is that biologically relevant features are likely to vary smoothly across the graph. In plain terms, relationships in the pathway graph should help organize the extracted representation. The method encodes both the graph and expression profiles as kernels, then applies a generalized form of canonical correlation analysis in the associated feature spaces.

The authors test the resulting features by predicting functional classes of genes in the yeast S. cerevisiae. A state-of-the-art classifier performs consistently better when given the extracted feature vectors than when given the original expression profiles. The reported result supports the usefulness of incorporating pathway structure into feature extraction for this prediction task.
neurips-2002-graph-driven-feature-extrac.tldr: Combining pathway graphs with gene expression data produces features that improve gene-function prediction in the reported yeast experiments.

paragraphs: Language acquisition has a distinctive feedback structure across generations. What one generation learns becomes the language input available to the next. This paper places that connection at the center of the learning problem, treating language acquisition and language change as linked processes rather than considering each learner's experience in isolation.

The connection creates an opportunity for languages to adapt to the characteristics of their learners. Each generation receives input shaped by earlier learning, and its own learned language contributes to the next generation's input. The language being acquired therefore participates in a continuing process of change, in which properties of learners can influence what later learners encounter.

The paper argues that this form of language change has important consequences for models of both the acquisition and evolution of syntax. Its central contribution is to bring transmission between generations into the explanation of learning. Understanding how syntax is acquired consequently involves considering how earlier acquisition has helped shape the input on which that learning operates.
neurips-2002-how-the-poverty-of-the-stim.tldr: Because each generation learns from the previous one, languages can adapt to learners, affecting theories of syntax acquisition and evolution.

paragraphs: When only a few examples have labels, a classifier must find a way to use the many examples that lack them. This paper formulates a regularization approach connecting the distribution of inputs to the conditional distribution of labels given inputs. That connection lets unlabeled examples impose additional constraints beyond those supplied by the labeled examples.

The regularization penalty measures information implied about labels over regions that cover the input space. It therefore links where the data occur with how the classifier distributes label probabilities across those regions. The formulation does not require a parametric model and remains tractable when the input distribution is represented by a continuous density.

The authors develop algorithms for finite collections of covering regions and establish a differential equation describing a limiting formulation. They illustrate the behavior of the approach in simple cases. The contribution is a general mathematical and algorithmic mechanism for incorporating the input distribution into classification when labels are only partially available.
neurips-2002-information-regularization-.tldr: Information regularization uses the input distribution to constrain label predictions when only some examples are labeled.

paragraphs: A dataset's intrinsic dimension describes the dimensionality of its underlying structure. This paper proposes an algorithm for estimating that dimension from the geometry of the observed data. As indicated by its title, the approach uses packing numbers, making geometric organization the basis for the estimate rather than a specified model of how the data were generated.

Two design features make the method straightforward to apply: it requires neither parametric assumptions about the generating process nor input parameters for the user to choose. These properties reduce the need to commit to a particular distributional model or configure the estimator before using it. They are part of the method's stated formulation.

The authors compare their estimator with a similar, widely used geometric algorithm. In the reported experiments, the proposed method is more robust to the data-generating distribution and more reliable in the presence of noise. These findings support its practical appeal within that comparison, particularly when estimating dimension from data whose geometry is affected by noisy observations.
neurips-2002-intrinsic-dimension-estimat.tldr: A parameter-free geometric dimension estimator shows greater robustness to distribution changes and noise than a related method in experiments.

paragraphs: A reflex reacts after its triggering sensory event has already occurred. This paper asks how a system can learn to act earlier when another sensory input predicts that event. It studies this question in a closed loop, where motor actions change the environment and thereby influence the sensory inputs the system subsequently receives.

The authors develop a linear learning algorithm and a systems-theoretic analysis of its behavior. Their analytical result shows that the studied system learns feed-forward control, replacing a slow feedback loop with an equivalent anticipatory controller. The availability of a predictive sensory input is central: it provides the information needed to generate an earlier response.

This creates a forward model of the reflex and turns the system's behavior from reactive to proactive. A robot implementation demonstrates the applicability of the theoretical results. The work connects learning and control by showing how a predictive cue can support earlier action within a system whose own movements influence what it senses.
neurips-2002-learning-a-forward-model-of.tldr: A linear learning rule lets a closed-loop system use predictive sensory cues to replace delayed reflex feedback with anticipatory control.

paragraphs: This paper introduces mismatch kernels for classifying proteins with support vector machines. The kernels compare protein sequences through shared short subsequences while allowing a bounded number of mismatches. Similarity can therefore reflect approximate local matches, giving the classifier a way to use related sequence patterns even when they are not identical.

The approach is discriminative and does not require a generative model of the positive training sequences. Its main computational device is a mismatch tree, a data structure used to calculate the kernels efficiently. Together, the similarity definition and efficient computation provide a direct route from protein sequences to an SVM-based classification method.

Experiments use a benchmark SCOP dataset for remote homology detection. The mismatch-kernel SVM performs as well as the Fisher kernel in that comparison while requiring considerably less computation. The result matters because it combines competitive classification performance with computational savings in the reported setting, showing that a sequence-based discriminative approach can be effective without fitting the stated generative model.
neurips-2002-mismatch-string-kernels-for.tldr: Mismatch kernels classify proteins using approximate subsequence matches, matching Fisher-kernel performance with substantial computational savings in the reported benchmark.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a model that learns a parts-based representation of high-dimensional data. Its key assumption is that the dimensions can be divided into disjoint groups, called factors, whose values vary independently. Each factor is assumed to have only a small number of discrete states, providing a compact description of its possible configurations.

The model represents each factor with a vector quantizer. An input is explained by the selected states of several factors, which act as its multiple causes. Learning determines both which dimensions belong to each factor and which states each factor can take. The decomposition and the representations of its parts are therefore learned together from training examples.

Variational algorithms make inference and learning efficient within this formulation. The authors present applications to image decomposition, collaborative filtering, and text classification. These examples illustrate how the same factor-based model can be used across different data types. Its interpretation rests on the stated independent, disjoint-factor structure, which defines how the learned parts combine to represent an input.
neurips-2002-multiple-cause-vector-quant.tldr: Multiple cause vector quantization learns independent groups of dimensions and discrete states that jointly provide a parts-based representation.

paragraphs: Music collections can contain both musical content and associated text, such as lyrics or contextual descriptions. This paper proposes a statistical approach that models the two together. The goal is to make their relationship useful for searching and browsing collections, including situations where a query contains both music and words.

The approach uses multimodal mixture models, with parameters learned through maximum a posteriori estimation using EM. Music and text are treated as parts of a shared statistical modeling problem. This gives the learned model a basis for connecting the two forms of content across documents and queries, rather than requiring a search request to use only one form.

The authors describe several uses for the learned models: browsing documents containing music and text, searching with mixed queries, adding music to text documents, and recommending or identifying similar songs. These capabilities give the joint model a broader role than song identification alone. Its contribution is a flexible probabilistic framework connecting musical and textual information across these retrieval and annotation tasks.
neurips-2002-name-that-song-a-probabilis.tldr: Joint probabilistic models of music and text support mixed queries, browsing, music annotation, and song recommendation.

paragraphs: Direct neural control of an external device requires translating brain activity into continuous movement estimates. This paper develops a real-time control system using spikes recorded from approximately 40 neurons in the arm area of primary motor cortex. The task involves moving a cursor to reach randomly positioned targets on a computer display.

The method explicitly models both hand motion and its probabilistic relationship with neuronal firing rates. A Kalman filter provides the framework for encoding and decoding these signals. This control-theoretic formulation connects the evolving movement to the observations used to estimate it, making the motion model part of the decoding process.

In offline experiments, the authors report more accurate hand-trajectory reconstructions than previously reported results. They also state that the model provides insight into how movement is represented in neural activity. The evidence therefore concerns reconstruction accuracy as well as interpretation of neural coding, with the reported accuracy improvement specifically established in the offline experiments.
neurips-2002-neural-decoding-of-cursor-m.tldr: A Kalman-filter decoder models hand motion and neural firing together, improving offline trajectory reconstruction in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning a probabilistic network often aims to recover its connections rather than just estimate its parameters. This paper examines how independent Dirichlet priors on parameters affect the structure learned for discrete variables. It focuses on the prior's scale parameter, commonly interpreted as prior strength or an equivalent number of observations.

The surprising result is that a small scale parameter produces strong structural regularization, favoring sparse graphs when the dataset is sufficiently large. As the scale approaches zero, the learned structure becomes the empty graph. This reverses the expectation that weakening the prior in this way would recover the complete graph associated with an unregularized maximum-likelihood estimate.

The parameter-level effect of the prior still behaves as expected. Consequently, its scale controls a trade-off between regularizing numerical parameters and regularizing network structure. The authors demonstrate predictive-accuracy benefits from optimizing that trade-off. The practical implication is that interpreting the scale solely as parameter-level prior strength can miss its substantial influence on which connections the model learns.
neurips-2002-on-the-dirichlet-prior-and-.tldr: Small Dirichlet scale parameters can strongly favor sparse network structures, creating a trade-off between parameter and structural regularization.

paragraphs: Address-event representation provides a way to communicate sparse neural events between neuromorphic chips. It also supports large networks whose synaptic connections can be configured. This paper extends that framework so the address domain can control synaptic plasticity as well, adding configurable changes in connection strength to its existing connectivity capabilities.

As a proof of concept, the authors implement a biologically inspired spike timing-dependent plasticity rule. Learning depends on the relative timing of events represented in the AER system. This connects the event-based communication framework to a learning mechanism, allowing temporal relationships among neural events to influence how the network's synapses change.

Experiments use an analog VLSI network of integrate-and-fire neurons on a task requiring neurons to group correlated inputs. The results demonstrate learning in the address domain for that task. The contribution is thus both an extension of the AER framework toward configurable plasticity and a hardware demonstration showing that a timing-based learning rule can operate within it.
neurips-2002-spike-timing-dependent-plas.tldr: An address-event framework gains configurable synaptic learning, demonstrated with spike timing-dependent plasticity in analog neural hardware.

paragraphs: Predicting behavior from cortical activity requires a useful way to compare neural recordings. This paper constructs biologically motivated kernels called Spikernels for sequences of neural population spike counts. A kernel supplies an inner-product comparison associated with an abstract feature space, allowing the recordings to be used in prediction tasks through that representation.

The authors explain how to derive these kernels and provide an efficient algorithm for evaluating a Spikernel on two sequences. The method therefore addresses both the definition of a neural-activity comparison and its computation. Its input is a sequence of spike counts, preserving a sequential representation of the recorded population activity.

The evaluation predicts hand movement velocities from cortical recordings and compares Spikernels with several standard kernels. In every reported experiment, all tested kernels outperform the ordinary scalar product used in regression, and the Spikernel performs best. These results support the value of the proposed representation for this decoding task, with the consistent advantage referring to the experiments reported in the paper.
neurips-2002-spikernels-embedding-spikin.tldr: Biologically motivated Spikernels compare neural spike-count sequences and perform best among the tested kernels for predicting hand velocity.

paragraphs: This paper connects several ways of comparing text by treating document generation as a staged Markov process. From that probabilistic model, the authors derive a Fisher kernel that can reconstruct n-gram and string kernels. The connection provides a common modeling perspective on methods that otherwise appear as separate definitions of document similarity.

That perspective also suggests how to make string kernels more flexible. Their parameters can reflect the statistics of the training collection, and the underlying process can include subsequences of different lengths. The authors give a procedure for identifying informative subsequences and constructing a finite-state machine from them, which then supplies another Fisher kernel.

The parameterization also controls how strongly individual features contribute, including a construction that yields logarithmic feature weighting. Experiments compare the resulting kernels with one another and with a bag-of-words baseline. The contribution is a probabilistic route for understanding, adapting, and extending sequence-based text kernels, including both the selection of features and the weights those features receive.
neurips-2002-string-kernels-fisher-kerne.tldr: A probabilistic Fisher-kernel view unifies text kernels and enables corpus-dependent weighting and informative subsequences of varying lengths.

paragraphs: Models of dopamine activity often interpret neuronal responses as reward prediction errors learned through temporal differences. This paper addresses how such models can retain useful information about cues whose consequences arrive later. The authors focus on two features of dopamine experiments: relevant states can be hidden, and the timing of events can vary.

Their model grounds temporal-difference learning in partially observable semi-Markov processes. Instead of representing sensory history through a tapped delay line, it infers the underlying state of the world. The dopamine system then learns reward predictions associated with those inferred states, combining uncertainty about the situation with learning about its expected consequences.

The authors report that this formulation can explain previously difficult observations of dopamine responses under temporal variability. Its significance is the connection between a process of state inference and a physiologically grounded reward-learning account. The model also brings ideas from more abstract psychological theories of behavior into contact with physiological observations, through a shared account of hidden state and timing.
neurips-2002-timing-and-partial-observab.tldr: A dopamine model combines hidden-state inference with temporal-difference learning to explain reward responses when event timing varies.

paragraphs: Images of the same scene can have different colors because lighting and certain camera settings change. The authors previously modeled these joint color changes statistically by measuring mappings between colors in paired images of a scene. This paper extends that color-flow model to handle changes that vary across different positions in an image.

The extension allows the color-flow coefficients to follow a low-order polynomial over image position. Instead of requiring the same coefficients everywhere, the model can express smooth spatial variation. This gives it greater flexibility for smoothly changing illumination and curved surfaces, while the low-order form keeps the additional capacity controlled.

The authors show results for image matching, shadow removal, and shadow detection. These applications use the model's treatment of appearance changes caused by lighting. The main contribution is a structured increase in spatial flexibility: color transformations can vary across an image without making that variation unrestricted, allowing the model to better fit the stated lighting and surface conditions.
neurips-2002-unsupervised-color-constanc.tldr: Spatially varying color-flow coefficients improve modeling of smooth lighting changes, with demonstrations in image matching and shadow processing.

paragraphs: Learning a dependency tree can be solved exactly with a spanning-tree algorithm once pairwise mutual information values are known. On large datasets, however, computing those values can dominate the total cost. This paper targets that bottleneck by letting the tree-building procedure operate with partial information about edge weights.

The algorithm maintains probabilistic confidence intervals derived from small data samples. When an interval is too broad for the tree-building process, the algorithm requests more data for that particular attribute pair. Computation is therefore directed toward refining the comparisons that need more evidence. The spanning-tree procedure relies entirely on Tarjan's red-edge rule.

Experiments show runtime that is nearly constant as the number of records grows, without a significant reduction in the accuracy of the resulting trees. This is an empirical finding about the reported tests. The broader contribution is the coordination of sampling and tree construction, so learning need not begin by fully computing every pairwise coefficient.
neurips-2002-using-tarjan-s-red-rule-for.tldr: A dependency-tree algorithm selectively refines sampled edge estimates, achieving near-constant runtime in dataset size in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Compressing a partially observable decision problem is useful only if the smaller representation still supports good decisions. This paper studies state-space compression with decision quality as its guiding concern. It focuses on policy evaluation: predicting the expected future reward associated with following a policy in the problem.

The authors observe that a compression preserving accurate policy evaluation will preserve decision quality. They derive sufficient conditions for that predictive accuracy and analyze the mathematical properties these conditions give to lossless linear compressions. These conditions provide a route to ensuring preservation; the stated result does not make them necessary for every useful compression.

The same analysis leads to an iterative procedure for finding useful linear compressions that allow some information loss. The authors also explain how structured representations of a POMDP can help identify compressions. The contribution connects what a compressed model retains to the rewards needed for decision-making, linking an exact preservation analysis to a procedure for constructing approximate representations.
neurips-2002-value-directed-compression-.tldr: Value-directed POMDP compression preserves decision-relevant reward predictions and uses that analysis to construct approximate linear representations.
